CHAPTER FIVE

DISCUSSION, CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS

5.1 Introduction

Chapter Four reported what the system does and what it measured. This chapter asks what
those results mean. It summarises the findings, interprets them against the expectations set in
Chapter One, states which objectives were met and which were only partly met, positions the
system against the systems reviewed in Chapter Two, sets out the advantages and the
challenges honestly, states what the work contributes, and describes what would have to change
for the system to be used in an election that matters.

5.2 Summary of findings

The evaluation produced five results worth carrying forward.

Proving a ballot is practical on ordinary hardware, and the cost grows slowly with the size of
the electorate. The circuit at national scale, a register of over a million voters, proves in about
nine seconds on a twelve-year-old two-core laptop without AVX2 support, against about six
seconds for a register a thousand times smaller. Verification is constant regardless of circuit
size.

Privacy costs about four times a transparent ballot on chain. A private ballot uses 305,390 gas
in steady state against 72,762 for a functionally equivalent contract without secrecy. The
232,628 gas difference is the pairing check, which is to say it is the privacy itself, priced.

The on-chain footprint of a ballot does not grow with the electorate. The transaction payload
is 388 bytes whether the register holds a thousand voters or a million.

On the intended network the cost per ballot is a fraction of a cent, while the identical
computation on Ethereum mainnet would cost around fourteen dollars. This gap, not any
cryptographic consideration, is what makes the Layer-2 target necessary rather than merely
convenient.

The system's privacy depends on operational discipline that the cryptography cannot supply.
